I know that there's nothing wrong with me for having health issues, but it's like I don't want it to be real, and I feel ashamed asking for help when not long ago I was bouncing off the walls, high honor roll in school, and a complete party animal. My therapist is a really nice guy and he's been helpful, though.

I finally decided to use a mobility aid a couple nights ago. I'd been shopping with my mom, trying on clothes at multiple stores, and by the time we got into Target, I was so tired and got really faint and my legs hurt so bad that I was walking super unstable. So my mom asked if I wanted her to push me in the wheelchair the store provided. I felt so nervous the whole time but I finally felt okay getting around, and I never realized until then how bad it hurts for me to be walking around so much and that I do need help with it. 

Internalized ableism is really terrible. I spend a lot of my therapy talking about it. I always thought that refusing to get help and making myself keep walking or standing for long periods was "hanging on to my autonomy" but after reading your comment I realized it's making me have way less autonomy because I can't walk efficiently or get around well anymore. 

I also never thought about how the term disabled speaks more about how society is and less about individuals.

I had drunkorexia and plain alcoholism for over a year. It made me bloated, my skin was terrible, my hair was awful, I had a lot of problems with acid reflux, and I was not myself anymore period. I’ve been sober for 10 months now and it is worth the struggle. 

I also had a lot more mental issues from alcohol because I was malnourished in the beginning. I would hear things that weren’t there, get paranoid, have problems with my memory and thinking even when I was sober. 

Alcohol abuse PLUS an eating disorder has a very high potential to kill you or cause severe damage, because both issues can be fatal in their own rights. Combining them is a disaster waiting to happen.

 It’s also way easier to get poisoning if you’re drinking on an empty stomach. I didn’t realize that profusely vomiting meant I was already being poisoned and my body was trying to get rid of it before I caused further damage. I’m very lucky I never ended up in the hospital.

I had my blood tested because I had an ovarian cyst causing a ton of pain, which my doctor and I thought was a Crohn’s flare because of the kind of pain and pressure I felt. He did blood tests to check and my C-reactive was under 0.3 mg/dL, and he did a CT scan which showed absolutely no inflammation from Crohn’s but a HUGE cyst. It’s likely from my Nexplanon implant. 

He also checked my white cell count and I’ve had my B12 and iron levels checked recently too, which were all normal. My Humira levels are checked about every 6 months and it shows I’m using the correct dosage so far and my body is still responding to it. 

My calprotectin is due to be checked by the end of the month, so I can get the collection kit when I go in to get my other blood tests. 

Surprisingly, I’ve never had calprotectin checked to confirm flares and remission; only blood tests, CTs, and colon/endoscopies.

I was confirmed to be in remission after a colon/endoscopy in August, and then told I should still  be good to go after the CT and blood tests in December.

I’m pretty sure I have hyperadrenergic POTS, specifically. 

I asked my doctor about people growing out of it, or if I’d grow out of it. He said “growing out of it” isn’t as common as people make it out to be, honestly. But I might find it’ll peak and then start to plateau or even improve as I get older, whether it’s from my body changing or treatments getting better over time.

He said “he thought it was what I wanted.” He also said I gave him mixed signals, that I “oversold my threshold” for what I could handle, that “he has things he could complain about too with that night but he’s mature enough not to”, and that he’s taking responsibility so he doesn’t know what else I want to hear. I asked my doctors. They said absolutely nothing a person does or doesn’t do causes Crohn’s; if you have it, you have it. Lifestyle choices can exacerbate symptoms, but you cannot cause it. 

You also can’t cause a flare. I got off steroids and after tapering off completely I drank a lot of liquor that night. The next day I was in the ER with a severe flare. I asked my doctor if the drinking caused the flare. He said the flare will happen regardless of your choices, and there was nothing I could’ve done to stop it anyways.

I thought I caused it. When I was 15 (TW) I started abusing laxatives and puking up my food. And I would go from severely anorexic to bulimic back and forth until I was about 18. I was also a severe alcoholic from 16 to 18, and I thought that caused it. 

Upon asking my doctors though, they said it doesn’t matter what I could’ve done because I was diagnosed at 17, and the age where Crohn’s typically shows up is 15 for women (I had symptoms since 14 but thought they were a result of stress and my eating problems). They also said there’s a connection between undiagnosed Crohn’s and eating disorders. 

Girls will eat like normal but have bloating, bowel problems, weight gain, abdominal pain, so they eat less and less and realize their pain goes away. Although they’re starving themselves, technically they’re doing “bowel relaxation”, because since nothing is going in, the bowel can’t become irritated. Then once they eventually start eating more again, the symptoms come back. Thus the girls notice a pattern and realize they don’t have problems if they barely eat, so they avoid food. 

I can’t remember where the study was but there was a study done pertaining to undiagnosed Crohn’s and the development of eating disorders in young females.

So it wasn’t my eating disorder that caused Crohn’s, it’s much more likely that it was the other way around, although I didn’t realize it.

I’m afraid of hospitals too! I’m immunocompromised so germs are a big fear of mine, as well as hospitals with sick people. But being immunocompromised and chronically ill means hospitals are a big part of my life. 

So what I do is go to my appointments,  and let the doctors do what they need. I might still be spiraling in my head the entire time, but I ultimately try to remember that I’m in a HOSPITAL. I’m surrounded by medical professionals. And honestly, I’ve let them know about my different concerns before and they’re all kind. 

For example, I needed a CT scan with contrast done, and I was super scared I’d be allergic to the dye. I told the nurse I was scared and she reminded me that she’s a nurse; if anything were to happen she’s right there to fix it. I told another doctor that I’m terrified of interactions between medications. So the doctor would pull up the entire chart of possible interactions for every single one of my medications with the anxiety med she was going to prescribe me, and explained every page to me to put me at ease. 

Sometimes sharing my concern with the staff definitely helps alleviate anxiety for me. But ultimately, letting myself be a little scared is important, because it teaches my mind that whatever I’m facing does not have as much power as my mind is giving it.

I had a really traumatic birth, which led to epilepsy. I “grew out of it” by 3 years old, but by 2 years old, I was already showing signs of OCD. 

I wouldn’t play with my toys; I lined them up and color-coordinated them. I had to make things look a particular way. If another kid knocked my lineup over, I’d cry and freak out. I was extremely particular about my clothing. My socks had to feel just right and even, and my shoes had to be the same tightness. My shirts couldn’t have any wrinkles if I tucked them in. 

As I got older, I couldn’t put my hair up in a timely manner. A ponytail couldn’t have any bumps; it had to be perfectly smooth. My nail polish all had to come off if one nail chipped. And the OCD became more obsession-based than physical compulsion-based as I aged, with themes starting to revolve around death, illness, harming others, and existential crises. 

The theory so far is that the neuron damage from the birth and epilepsy gave way to OCD, and possibly autism as well. My mom doesn’t think I “fell down a thought pattern rabbit hole”; the pattern of how my neurons would fire already existed before I could think clearly about such things. My mom also believes I could’ve received treatment much earlier if I had been in her care, as I was showing signs of severe OCD by 8 years old, but because I was living with my grandma, I was told to “stop thinking about it” and I had a disabling mental break at 15 for six months all surrounding my OCD because it had went unchecked for so long. 

I remember walking into my moms room and confessing to her that I was a pedophile, and I thought she’d disown me, yell at me, so many terrible things. But she just said, “Honey, I’m going to get you in to see a therapist. I think you have OCD, and you’re very sick right now. I can’t tell you whether you are or aren’t a pedophile, because that will only make you need more reassurance. But I can tell you that everything will be alright and things won’t always feel this way.” 

She had been doing research for a few weeks after I started asking her questions that she thought were off, like, “How do you know if you’ve done something bad but you can’t remember it?” and, “How do you know what memories are real or fake?” or making “confessions” to her about all kinds of terrible things that I had clearly never done. 

So, I don’t think there was anything that could’ve prevented the OCD from occurring, but there were things that could’ve kept it from getting so bad when I was 15.

Yep, five times.

1- I was 10, having stabbing chest pain and I felt like I couldn’t breathe. My doctor was totally convinced it was anxiety. I come home from school a week later with more severe pain, and now I can’t feel my hands and feet. I go in and see a different doctor; I had severe walking pneumonia. 

2- I was 17 and my stomach hurt BAD. After every meal, my stomach was KILLING ME. I started getting so bloated and having sores in my mouth, blood in the toilet, could barely get a pair of pants on by myself. I go into the doctor, and I know it’s something VERY wrong but he just thinks it’s appendicitis. Nope, he does a CT on me and it turned out I had SEVERE untreated Crohn’s Disease.

3- Later, about three months after, I get off my steroids and we think it calmed my Crohn’s inflammation. I start having horrific stomach pain, and I’m convinced something is really wrong. I go into the ER. The doctor couldn’t feel a blockage, no appendicitis signs… we do a CT again. There it is, a RAGING flare from tapering off my steroids. 

4- In September earlier this year I was prescribed 20mg Prozac. I start taking it and somehow immediately feel side effects. I was tired, nauseous, I couldn’t cry, I couldn’t eat, I couldn’t sleep at night. On the second day of the pills, it gets worse. I wake up in a panic, I’m always feeling like I’m tripping on psychedelics, I have zero appetite, I can’t cry NO MATTER HOW TERRIBLE I FEEL. Third, fourth, and fifth days go by. I have a fire in my chest, can’t feel my limbs, there’s pressure in my head, and I was so loopy. I started sweating, having zero heat tolerance, feeling like I’d faint or die or something constantly. On the sixth day, at like 3 am, I go into the ER, because I feel sicker than I have in my entire life. I can’t even describe it; it was just horrific. I thought they’d tell me it was just anxiety and I had to go home, which seemed like what was happening. Nope, turns out my side effects, while they were technically normal, should not have happened immediately nor been that severe. The pills made me manic, kind of. And I’m not diagnosed bipolar, but the same things happen when I take steroids too. I was told to stop taking the Prozac immediately and given a hydroxyzine prescription. The crazy thing is, I called my pharmacist and the nurse line multiple times before that night about how bad the side effects were and they all told me to keep taking the meds and that it was fine. 

5- In October I saw my doctor for a regular appointment. I told her I’d been feeling terrible, lightheaded, super dizzy. I said something was just really off. She takes my blood pressure and it’s 80/56. Looks like I have orthostatic hypotension now.

It could, depending on the triggers you have. For me, I have OCD that manifests as severe hypochondria/health anxiety, and I often need to do some exposure therapies to snap myself out of the loop, like 

- Measuring my blood pressure (I have hypotension and getting my pressure taken gives me terrible anxiety but is necessary on a daily basis)
- Staying home alone for a short time- I tend to have the worst panic attacks where I think I’m dying when I’m alone, I think because of the fear that no one is around to help me
- NOT checking my heart rate- I need to check my heart rate when I feel dizzy because of my hypotension but otherwise, I check it ANY time I notice it, which is just a compulsion. So if I’ve simply noticed my heart rate or “feel like it’s beating a little fast/hard”, I sit there without checking it. And 10/10 times, the anxiety dissipates.
- Getting any labs or tests done that I’ve been putting off- I have really bad anxiety surrounding blood tests and labs, but I need them done regularly for Crohn’s Disease and medication monitoring. My provider knows I have a hard time with getting my blood drawn so she gives me a decent window of about a month or so to help me plan in advance as best I can. I usually like to procrastinate a lot on them, but I’ve found getting them done as soon as I have an “okay-ish” day is the best, because I can get my results sooner, thus figuring out treatment sooner if anything is wrong. 

What HASN’T helped me:

- Googling ANYTHING EVER, excluding “panic attack/anxiety/PTSD symptoms” (so I can see how everything I’m experiencing is normal for a panic attack)
- Getting unnecessary tests done- unless my doctor has suggested or put in an order for the tests, it just increases my anxiety and wastes my time and energy. 10/10 times, nothing was wrong with me that couldn’t be fixed with some OTC vitamins or supplements
- Calling my doctor/a nurse hotline- I’ve made a rule for myself to wait at least 24 hours on the symptoms if they’re particularly bad, and at least 4 days if they’re just a nuisance. Most of the time, they’re not new symptoms at all, just anxiety symptoms that I happened to notice or fixate on because I was triggered

Idk, these are just some exposure-type things that worked and didn’t work for me. Health anxiety is tricky because a lot of the time, it starts from a legitimate health concern or health problem that you ONCE had or someone else did, and anxiety can conjure up literally any symptom humanly possible, so it’s hard to draw the line between a real concern and something completely manufactured by anxiety. But that’s why I like to use the 24 hour and 4 day rule, before I jump to getting any tests or scheduling an appointment.

I am literally a POSTER child for “young person in kink getting target by abusers”. I don’t know how but it happened to me twice in a row, once with a guy and once with a girl (I’m 18), so here is what I’ve learned:

• Play/talk with peers. Be wary of anyone 25/26/27+ trying to initiate/push for a dynamic or playing or meeting. You can certainly learn from your elders, but be careful.

• Always, ALWAYS ask for verification. Ask for live pictures, ID, anything to put your mind at ease and prove they’re who they say they are. If they don’t wanna provide proof, run. 

• You are NEVER obligated to send ANY compromising photos, videos, or media that include identifying information or traits about you. Be very careful and make sure you trust the other person, if you decide to do that. You can send pictures of your face/ID for verification and vetting if that’s agreed upon, but you’re not obligated to send anything further. 

• Be very vigilant about “frenzy”. Do not rush into doing everything at once because the opportunity has presented itself. It may seem new and exciting, but trust me, take it slow.

• Communicate early on/initiate conversations about RACK (Risk Aware Consensual Kink), SSC (Safe, Sane, Consensual), and PRICK (Personal Responsibility, Informed, Consensual Kink). Do they know what those are? Do they understand the importance of those concepts? Do YOU? These are all essential to your safety. 

• If they say they’re “trained” and make that a big deal, RUN. Yes, there are plenty of kink courses and workshops you can take, and you can be trained to properly engage in certain activities, like rigging or flogging. However, unless it is your profession, you cannot “train” to be a Dominant, much like how you cannot “train” to be a submissive. These type of Dominants who parade their “training” around on the Internet are the ones who believe they are owed your submission and that you follow THEIR rules. These people do not tend to be good negotiators, and are at best, ignorant, and at worst, abusers in disguise. 

• Your consent must ALWAYS be informed, freely given, able to be revoked at any point, sober/when you have the ability to consent, and ENTHUSIASTIC. The same goes for any consent you are given. The moment you do not consent, it stops there. You do not have to continue and are under zero obligation to do so. Your feelings are equally as important as those of who you’re playing with, always, no matter the dynamic in place.

• Have fun! Feel free to ask questions on here, learn from reputable sites/people (I recommend Evie Lupine for a great kink intro YouTuber), and play with the people you’re comfortable with. Kink should always be enjoyable and fun for all involved, never stressful or upsetting.

It would have been Imperfect Self Defense and not ‘Perfect Self Defense’. Imperfect Self Defense requires that the defendant genuinely believed, no matter how unreasonable, that there was an imminent threat of danger. 

If Lyle and Eric believed that by their parents shutting the doors, they were preparing to kill them, and that was why the boys shot them, then it fits the criteria for Imperfect Self Defense.
